researcher: Codex parallel north-africa research, integrated by Codex

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Art of the Fatimid Period, 909 to 1171
sources.note: Suzan Yalman, 2001. Dynastic origins, North African capitals, Cairo, workshops and monuments.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Masterpieces from the Department of Islamic Art
sources.note: Printed pages 137 and 145; catalogue 93, Bowl with Eagle (63.178.1), Arabic signature and Fatimid ending.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Rock-crystal Decorative Element, 17.190.522a
sources.note: Object details: ninth to tenth century, attributed to Egypt; proposed perfume-container function and later European reuse.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Gold earring, 1978.142.1
sources.note: Object details: eleventh-century Egypt; gold wire, filigree and granulation.

sources.title: Cambridge University Library: Rhubarb and dodder and absinth, Or.1081 J39
sources.note: Efraim Lev and Leigh Chipman, 2011. Eleventh- to twelfth-century prescription; languages, rose syrup and diet. Proposed identification of patient is uncertain.

sources.title: Cambridge University Library: Medicine in the Cairo Genizah, introduction
sources.note: Collection context and medical fragments; documents represent particular people and surviving texts, not all Egyptian households.

sources.title: Princeton Geniza Project: Bodleian MS heb. b 11/7, document 519
sources.note: Primary Judaeo-Arabic letter with edited transcription and translation; reused Fatimid fiscal account dated 500 AH (1106 to 1107) supplies earliest possible date.

sources.title: Cambridge University Library: Mevorakh ibn Yazdad and a child’s inheritance
sources.note: Fragment of the Month, 2017; appointment about 1019 to supervise guardians and subsequent litigation.

sources.title: Corisande Fenwick: How to Found an Islamic State: The Idrisids
sources.note: 2022 chapter, printed pages 91 to 116; political formation, coinage, domestic complex and limits of later narratives.

sources.title: Fentress, Fenwick and Limane: Urban life in early Islamic Morocco
sources.note: Archaeology International 25(1), 2022, pages 111 to 131. Idrisid housing, wells, metalworking and destruction contexts, especially pages 126 to 128.

sources.title: Penn, Fenwick and Limane: Gaming in the Maghreb al-Aqsa
sources.note: 2026 archaeological study; bathhouse board and separately excavated bone dice. Exact game identification and older excavation contexts remain uncertain.

sources.title: Volubilis archaeological project: INSAP/UCL excavations
sources.note: Current excavations and 2000 to 2005 results: modest houses, family silos and much larger storage in the elite complex.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Medina of Fez
sources.note: Outstanding Universal Value: paired early quarters, later unification, Marinid capital and surviving institutions.

sources.title: Furkan Erbaş: Fatimid-Idrisid Relations, 909 to 985
sources.note: Tokat İlmiyat Dergisi 12(1), 2024, pages 260 to 275; abstract and conclusion on shifting Fatimid/Umayyad dominance and final defeat.

sources.title: Jordan Ahli Bank: Islamic Coins collection catalogue
sources.note: Printed page 230, Idris II silver coin, catalogue 1; Arabic transcription including Ali. Mint/date readings in catalogue are qualified.

sources.title: Museum With No Frontiers: Marinid dynasty
sources.note: Dynastic account: Zenata origins, Fez Jdid, eastward expansion and subsequent fragmentation.

sources.title: Museum With No Frontiers: Buinaniya Madrasa, Fez
sources.note: Architecture and functions; built in the 1350s. The entry gives differing converted completion years, so the card uses the decade.

sources.title: Batha Museum: Marinid house door, 45.110
sources.note: Fourteenth-century Fez house door; materials, gate, knockers and purchase from the ruins of a Marinid house.

sources.title: Batha Museum: Al-Misbahiya ceiling fragment, 45.103
sources.note: Carved and painted cedar from the Fez madrasa built in 1346 to 1347; recovered during restoration.

sources.title: Batha Museum: Excised zellij from Buinaniya, C18
sources.note: Fourteenth-century tilework, technique and twentieth-century restoration recovery.

sources.title: Ludovic Liétard: Two New Marinid Coins Struck in Azammur
sources.note: Journal of the Oriental Numismatic Society 231, Spring 2018, printed pages 19 to 20, figures 3 and 4: half dirham, Arabic transcription and translation; final Marinid ruler and 1465 rebellion.

sources.title: Bavarian State Library: Quran volume, Cod.arab. 3
sources.note: Last volume of a twelve-part Quran associated with Marinid Abu Yaqub Yusuf, 1286 to 1307; parchment and Maghribi script.

sources.title: A. R. Disney: A History of Portugal and the Portuguese Empire, volume 2, excerpt
sources.note: Cambridge University Press excerpt, North Africa: Asilah 1471, Wattasid accession in Fez 1472, coastal trade and Mamora 1515.

sources.title: Mercedes García-Arenal: Sainteté et pouvoir dynastique au Maroc
sources.note: Study of Fez and Saadian power; note 4 on Wattasid chronology, note 15 on Marmol’s account of Medgara agriculture and refugees.

sources.title: Jocelyne Dakhlia: La vie morale des sociétés musulmanes
sources.note: Discussion of Wattasid to Saadian transmission of court knowledge, including al-Arifa bint Nedjju and Qasim al-Zerhuni.

sources.title: National Library of Morocco: Wattasid-period Quran, 1304
sources.note: Fifteenth- to sixteenth-century Moroccan manuscript, incomplete part of a twelve-volume set; silver writing on green paper and gold headings. Dating is stylistic.

sources.title: Numista: Quarter dirham of Abu al-Abbas Ahmad, N480827
sources.note: Photographed collector specimen, attributed to Ahmad, 1526 to 1545; Arabic legends and reference to Album 550. No excavation provenance or minted year is supplied.

sources.title: A Moroccan Amir’s Commercial Treaty with Venice of the Year 913/1508
sources.note: Study of the treaty with the quasi-independent ruler of Badis, a Wattasid cousin; port politics and diplomatic record.

sources.title: Leo Africanus: History and Description of Africa, volume 2
sources.note: Digitized primary account in John Pory’s English translation, edited by Robert Brown, Hakluyt Society 1896; printed pages 424 to 425, lectures and student support. A later English edition of a sixteenth-century account, not a census.

sources.title: Royal Library of El Escorial: Muley Zaydan’s Quran
sources.note: Patrimonio Nacional, manuscript Arabic 1340: copied at Marrakech in 1599 for Saadian Muley Zaydan; later entered El Escorial.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum: Western North Africa, 1600 to 1800
sources.note: Chronology: transition from Saadian to Alaouite rule in the seventeenth century and later Moroccan state.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Historic City of Meknes
sources.note: Outstanding Universal Value: Moulay Ismail’s capital, walls and distinct medina/kasbah ensembles; buildings span several dynasties. The brief description misleadingly calls Ismail the dynasty’s founder, a claim not used here.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Medina of Essaouira
sources.note: Outstanding Universal Value: eighteenth-century royal port, planning, trading links and multiple communities.

sources.title: Chouki El Hamel: The Register of the Slaves of Sultan Mawlay Ismail
sources.note: Journal of African History 51(1), 2010, pages 89 to 98; archival register and coerced enslavement of free Black Moroccans.

sources.title: Batha Museum: Dish decorated with inscription, 54.794
sources.note: First half of nineteenth century, Fez; stylised al-mulk inscription, ceramic pigments and proposed decorative function.

sources.title: Batha Museum: Dish 54.794, Arabic catalogue entry
sources.note: Arabic description explicitly transcribes الملك and interprets divine power; sample is normalised type, not a facsimile of mirrored Kufic.

sources.title: Batha Museum: Batta jug, 46.1.1018
sources.note: Nineteenth-century Fez or Meknes lamp-oil jug, purchased in Fez; different decoration for southern and urban markets.

sources.title: United States Office of the Historian: Morocco
sources.note: Diplomatic history: 1786 treaty, 1821 Tangier building gift, 1912 protectorate and 1956 independence.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Rabat, Modern Capital and Historic City
sources.note: Planned capital developed under the French Protectorate, especially 1912 to 1930; modern city beside older fabric, continuing heritage management.

sources.title: Constitute Project: Morocco’s 2011 Constitution, Arabic text
sources.note: Articles 1, 4 and 5; constitutional description, state motto and official status of Arabic and Amazigh. Constitutional statements are distinguished from empirical outcomes.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Heritage: Knowledge and practices concerning couscous
sources.note: 2020 multinational inscription for Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia; preparation, equipment, shared meals and learning.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Heritage: Argan practices and know-how
sources.note: 2014 inscription: southwest Morocco, processing, women’s knowledge, transmission and social uses.

sources.title: UNESCO Intangible Heritage: Gnawa
sources.note: 2019 inscription; historical links with slavery, music, rituals, instruments and modern transmission.

sources.title: World Bank and partner development banks: Noor Ouarzazate solar complex
sources.note: March 2017 project brief: Noor I commissioned in February 2016 with 160 MW; later projects and forecast figures are distinguished from completed outcomes.

sources.title: Qiyas Şükürov: Vattasiler, TDV Encyclopedia of Islam
sources.note: Specialist reference, 2012; final paragraphs on Fez in 1549, Abu Hassun’s recovery and death in September 1554.

sources.title: United Nations Decolonization: Western Sahara
sources.note: UN territory record: listed as a Non-Self-Governing Territory since 1963. The imported map cannot resolve sovereignty.

batchIdentityNotes.note: Index 1000 to 1279; border features repeat a broad North Africa/Egypt/Levant polygon through 1279, well beyond the historical 1171 ending. No polygon fix proposed. Card explicitly separates actual history from imported interval.

Index 800 to 1000, broad western Maghreb geometry. Prefer dynasty rather than caliphate. Historical formation 788 to 789 and contested tenth-century decline are distinct from imported dates. Coins and Walila excavations are local evidence, not verification of the full polygon.

Index 1300 to 1492, northern Moroccan polygon. Overlaps the already published thin merinides card, which this batch does not modify. This missing record covers the later Marinid period and post-1465 transition, so it receives its own dated card rather than an automatic alias.

Same named dynasty with spelling variants and adjacent imported windows: 1492 to 1530 and 1530 to 1650. First polygon covers northern Morocco; second extends farther south. Shared historical card is warranted, but 1530 is not a dynastic boundary and 1554 to 1650 is known mislabelled map time. No claim of accurate common geometry.

1650 to 1938 imported phase. Earliest geometry extends down to approximately 15 degrees north near the Niger bend; subsequent polygons differ, and later intervals cross the 1912 protectorate change. These broad imported outlines have not been historically validated. No suggestion that the Alaouites founded Morocco in 1650 or ended in 1938.

1960 to open ended. Modern geometry from 2020 extends into Western Sahara unlike earlier snapshots. Do not treat this source geometry as verification of sovereignty or a settled boundary. Card does not equate every mapped area with an uncontested national territory.

Writing sample uses the photographed, transcribed Numista collector record N480827 with its Album 550 reference. It is not an excavated museum coin; provenance and exact minting year remain unestablished. Original-script sample and attribution should receive independent review.
